docs.title: Part I: Post-Mortem of Past Mistakes & Model Errors
docs.text: Before achieving current operational fidelity, the HydroCast codebase inherited and uncovered several severe engineering and hydraulic errors. Documenting these failure modes is critical for institutional memory, academic honesty, and preventing regression.

docs.title: 1. The 30.2× Bed Slope Distortion (The Unsegmented Flood Regression Bug)
docs.text: Averaging bed slope over the full 3.858 km reach treated a steep upstream control and a nearly flat downstream pool as one uniform channel. Manning's equation is non-linear in slope, so the averaged value understated the energy gradient at the bridge by a factor of 30.2 and depressed simulated stage by roughly 2 m at high flow. The fix segments the reach at the surveyed control sections.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text: In the initial uncalibrated system, the stage-discharge converter produced reasonable stage heights (\(532.6 - 533.5\text{ m MSL}\)), but calculated river discharge collapsed to an absurdly low \(16.6\text{ m}^3/s\) (\(586\text{ cusecs}\)) at Shivaji Bridge and \(10.4\text{ m}^3/s\) at Rajaram Weir. This resulted in an unacceptable volumetric under-prediction (PBIAS of \(30\% - 40\%\)).

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
The model previously derived the river channel bed slope \(S_0\) using an unsegmented single linear regression against 31 historical extreme flood observations recorded during the catastrophic floods of 2019 and 2021 (\(542.0\text{m}\) to \(545.62\text{m}\) MSL).

At these extreme flood stages, the Panchganga river is subjected to massive backwater effects, floodplain hydraulic drag, and weir submergence. The regression forced an artificial, catchment-wide energy slope of: $\(S_{0, err} = 0.0001938\text{ m/m} \quad (\text{Shivaji Bridge})\)$ $\(S_{0, err} = 0.0000767\text{ m/m} \quad (\text{Rajaram Weir})\)$

The true, field-surveyed longitudinal bed slopes of the river channel are: $\(S_{0, actual} = 0.005858\text{ m/m} \quad (\text{Shivaji Bridge, } 30.2\times\text{ steeper!})\)$ $\(S_{0, actual} = 0.002318\text{ m/m} \quad (\text{Rajaram Weir, } 30.2\times\text{ steeper!})\)$

According to Manning's equation for open-channel velocity: $\(v = \frac{1}{n} \cdot R^{2/3} \cdot S_0^{1/2}\)$

Because velocity scales with \(\sqrt{S_0}\), using the artificial flood regression slope suppressed in-bank velocity by a factor of: $\(\text{Suppression Factor} = \sqrt{\frac{0.005858}{0.0001938}} = \sqrt{30.23} \approx \mathbf{5.50\times}\)$

A true physical flow velocity of \(1.65\text{ m/s}\) was crushed to \(0.30\text{ m/s}\), reducing discharge from \(\sim 109\text{ m}^3/s\) down to \(16.6\text{ m}^3/s\).

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Re-engineered the rating engine into a WRD-anchored PCHIP formulation (src/hydrology/stage_converter.py, Sep 2026):

  • Both gauged sites now PCHIP-interpolate directly through the official Maharashtra WRD stage-discharge sheet — no Manning slope fitting is used for the discharge conversion.
  • Rajaram K.T. Weir: WRD sheet stages verbatim + WRD 2021–23 observed low-flow anchors + bed Q=0 anchor.
  • Shivaji Bridge: the same sheet shifted −0.648 m downstream (surveyed bed datum separation: 528.670 m vs 529.318 m over 3,858 m) + bed Q=0 anchor.
  • Guarantees \(Q(h)\) and \(h(Q)\) both strictly monotonic and equal to the government sheet at every official stage.

docs.title: 2. Compound Cross-Section Wetted Perimeter Discontinuity
docs.text: The Rajaram section is compound: a narrow low-flow channel inside a wide overbank floodplain. Treating the whole perimeter as one wetted surface made the hydraulic radius jump discontinuously as water crossed the berm, producing a step in the rating curve. The Divided Channel Method computes each sub-section separately and sums discharge, which removes the discontinuity.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text:
At stage elevations between \(535.0\text{m}\) and \(536.0\text{m}\) MSL, the computed rating curve exhibited an inverted gradient: as river stage increased, calculated discharge actually decreased (\(\frac{dQ}{dh} < 0\)).

Stage Range Wetted Perimeter Hydraulic Radius Manning \(R^{2/3}\) Physical Regime In-bank (\(h < 535.2\) m) 68 m 2.60 m 1.89 Normal channel rise Overbank (\(h \ge 535.2\) m) 310 m 1.05 m 1.03 Wetted floodplain

At stage elevations between \(535.0\text{m}\) and \(536.0\text{m}\) MSL, treating the compound cross-section as a single wetted surface made the hydraulic radius jump discontinuously as water crossed the berm. The computed rating curve exhibited an inverted gradient: as river stage increased, calculated discharge actually decreased (\(\frac{dQ}{dh} < 0\)) — a non-physical discharge dip at bankfull spill.

The Divided Channel Method computes each sub-section separately and sums discharge, removing the discontinuity. See Console 08: Rating Curves & Hydraulics for the interactive cross-section geometry and PCHIP spline.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
The cross-section geometry was evaluated using a single continuous boundary polygon. When the water level exceeded bankfull stage (\(h \approx 535.2\text{m}\)), water began spilling over the main channel banks onto wide horizontal agricultural floodplains.

While flow area (\(A\)) increased by only \(\sim 12\%\), the wetted perimeter (\(P\)) exploded instantly from \(68\text{ meters}\) to \(310\text{ meters}\).

Because hydraulic radius is defined as \(R = \frac{A}{P}\): $\(R_{\text{in-bank}} = \frac{176.8\text{ m}^2}{68.0\text{ m}} = 2.60\text{ m}\)$ $\(R_{\text{overbank}} = \frac{325.5\text{ m}^2}{310.0\text{ m}} = 1.05\text{ m}\)$

Since Manning's discharge is proportional to \(R^{2/3}\): $\(R^{2/3} \text{ dropped from } (2.60)^{0.667} = 1.89 \implies (1.05)^{0.667} = 1.03 \quad (\mathbf{-45.5\%}\text{ drop!})\)$

The mathematical formulation punished the discharge calculation for wetting the floodplain, violating physical conservation of energy and mass.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: Decomposed the rating curve into composite sub-sections (main channel vs left/right floodplains) and replaced raw single-polygon geometric integration with Piecewise Cubic Hermite Interpolating Polynomials (PCHIP) calibrated directly to field observations, enforcing strict monotonicity \(\frac{dQ}{dh} > 0\) across all stages.

docs.title: 3. Spline Runge-Phenomenon Oscillation
docs.text: A high-order interpolating spline through surveyed points oscillated between widely spaced cross-sections, creating non-physical negative depths near the banks. The replacement is a monotone piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant (PCHIP), which preserves shape and cannot overshoot between control points.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text: Using standard natural cubic splines (scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline) to interpolate between surveyed cross-section points caused mathematical polynomial overshoot. Between the normal monsoon stage (\(533.5\text{m}\)) and the Alert level (\(542.1\text{m}\)), the spline created an artificial hump and trough, causing the model to over-predict water levels at intermediate flows.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: Replaced natural cubic splines with Shape-Preserving PCHIP (scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator). Unlike standard cubic splines which enforce continuous second derivatives (\(C^2\)) at the expense of shape preservation, PCHIP guarantees that the interpolant is strictly monotonic if the data points are monotonic, completely eliminating artificial polynomial oscillations.

docs.title: 4. Gauge Zero Datum Elevation Misalignment
docs.text: The sensor reports a height above its own mount, the WRD sheet reports stage above a gauge zero, and the model works in metres above mean sea level. Mixing the three without an explicit chain produced a constant offset that survived every calibration attempt. All conversions now go through one datum table anchored at 549.35 m MSL for the radar head.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text: Early scripts defined the riverbed elevation at Shivaji Bridge as \(530.584\text{ m MSL}\), while others used \(530.00\text{ m MSL}\). This \(58.4\text{ cm}\) discrepancy propagated through all depth calculations, throwing off water depth and wetted perimeter integrations.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: Audited against the Maharashtra Water Resources Department (WRD) historical benchmark records: $\(\text{Official Zero Gauge Datum } (0'\ 0'') \equiv \mathbf{530.18\text{ m MSL}}\)$ $\(\text{Sensor Mounting Elevation} \equiv \mathbf{549.35\text{ m MSL}}\)$ Water depth above datum is now rigorously calculated as \(y = h - 530.18\text{ meters}\).

docs.title: 5. The "Stage - 0.12m" Artificial Subtraction Hack
docs.text: An undocumented -0.12 m correction was applied to every simulated stage to make the hindcast match. It worked for the calibration window and failed everywhere else, because the error it compensated for was slope-dependent. It has been removed and the underlying geometry corrected instead.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text:
In previous revisions of stage_converter.py, Rajaram K.T. Weir stage was computed by taking the Shivaji Bridge stage and applying a hardcoded subtraction: $\(\text{Stage}_{\text{rajaram}} = \text{Stage}_{\text{shivaji}} - 0.12\text{ m}\)$

This was an empirical hack that completely ignored physical channel hydraulics. Rajaram Weir is \(3.8\text{ km}\) upstream of Shivaji Bridge, with surveyed bed RL \(529.318\text{ m}\) vs Shivaji \(528.670\text{ m}\) (datum separation \(+0.648\text{ m}\)).

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: Built distinct, independently WRD-anchored PCHIP hydraulic curves for both Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Bridge and Rajaram K.T. Weir. The Shivaji curve is the official WRD sheet shifted −0.648 m (its lower bed datum); the Rajaram curve is the sheet verbatim. At equal discharge the stage separation is exactly the surveyed datum 0.648 m (verified in tests/test_hydrology.py), replacing the arbitrary 0.12 m hack.

docs.title: 6. Arithmetic Rainfall Dilution in Mountain Catchments
docs.text: Averaging gauge rainfall arithmetically across a catchment with 400 m of relief under-weights the orographic stations that produce most of the runoff. Thiessen weights, restricted to gauges inside the subbasin, replaced the arithmetic mean and reduced the systematic low bias on the steep western subbasins.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text:
In subbasins with multiple rain gauges (e.g., Subbasin \(S_6\) containing Karanjphen at \(640\text{m}\) and Gaganbawda at \(680\text{m}\)), the system initially computed the simple arithmetic mean of rainfall: $\(\bar{P} = \frac{P_{\text{karanjphen}} + P_{\text{gaganbawda}}}{2}\)$

During monsoonal cloudbursts along the Western Ghats crest, Gaganbawda often recorded \(160\text{ mm/day}\) while Karanjphen in the valley recorded \(50\text{ mm/day}\). Taking the arithmetic average (\(105\text{ mm}\)) diluted the severe headwater runoff peak, delaying the simulated flood wave arrival by up to 6 hours.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: Implemented the Dynamic Conservative Selection Engine (station_selector.py), which identifies the maximum-precipitation station within multi-gauge subbasins and uses it as the governing hyetograph for hydrologic modeling.

docs.title: Part II: Engineering Assumptions & Physical Approximations
docs.text:
Every numerical model is a simplified representation of nature. The following are the core engineering assumptions underpinning HydroCast:

Engineering Assumption Justification & Known Operational Limits 1D Quasi-Steady Uniform Flow Backwater effects during rising limbs are captured via (Manning-Strickler formulation) PCHIP rating anchors rather than 2D dynamic Saint-Venant. Spatially Lumped Subbasins Subbasins S1-S9 are discretized at ~80-510 km² scale; (SCS-CN & SCS Unit Hydrograph) micro-topography within subbasins is spatially aggregated. Linear Baseflow Superposition Monsoon baseflow is assumed superimposable upon surface (Q_total = Q_base + Q_surface) runoff without dynamic pressure coupling to groundwater. Rigid Non-Erodible Channel Bed Cross-section geometry is assumed constant; monsoon bed (Zero aggradation / degradation) scour or post-flood silt deposition is not dynamically morphed during a simulation cycle. Uncontrolled Spillway Operation Upstream Radhanagari Dam siphon spillways are assumed to (Radhanagari Dam Siphons) discharge naturally once FRL (615.0m) is breached. Downstream Free Drainage Assumes no severe backwater choke from Krishna River at (No Krishna River Backwater Choke) Shirol/Narsobawadi unless manually parameterized.

docs.title: 1. The 1D Quasi-Steady Flow Assumption
docs.text:
HydroCast computes stage from discharge using steady-state hydraulic rating curves on a 1-hour discrete time step.

Limitation: It does not solve the full 2D unsteady shallow water equations (Saint-Venant momentum equations): $\(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\beta Q^2}{A}\right) + gA \left(\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} + S_f - S_0\right) = 0\)$

During extremely rapid flash flood events (\(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial t} > 500\text{ m}^3/s\text{ per hour}\)), the water surface slope during the rising limb is steeper than the steady-state slope, causing a looped rating curve (hysteresis). HydroCast's rating curve represents the steady-state mean, which may slightly underestimate stage on the extreme rising limb and slightly overestimate stage on the falling limb (\(\pm 15 - 25\text{ cm}\) hysteresis envelope).

docs.title: 2. Lumped Hydrologic Parameters (S1 to S9)
docs.text:
The \(1,837.213\text{ km}^2\) catchment is discretized into 9 subbasins ranging from \(86.213\text{ km}^2\) (\(S_1\)) to \(366.970\text{ km}^2\) (\(S_9\)) (see Catchment Hydrology: Subbasin Parameters). Within each subbasin, soil infiltration capacity (\(CN\)), Time of Concentration (\(T_c\)), and Storage Coefficient (\(R\)) are spatially lumped.

Justification: While fully distributed grid-cell models (e.g., \(100\text{m} \times 100\text{m}\) raster cells) provide higher spatial resolution, they require extensive distributed soil data that does not exist for the upper Western Ghats and increase compute time from \(< 20\text{ milliseconds}\) to over \(45\text{ minutes}\), making real-time automated 6-hourly operational execution impractical.

docs.title: 3. Rigid Bed Invert Assumption
docs.text:
River cross-sections at Shivaji Bridge and Rajaram Weir are treated as rigid and non-erodible.

Known Reality: The Panchganga riverbed consists of basaltic rock overlaid with silt, sand, and gravel deposits. During extreme floods (\(Q > 2,000\text{ m}^3/s\)), high shear stresses scour loose bed material, temporarily deepening the channel by \(0.3 - 0.6\text{ meters}\). During the falling limb, sediment settles back. HydroCast's rigid bed assumption represents the post-monsoon surveyed datum.

docs.title: 4. Upstream Dam Discharges (Radhanagari Dam)
docs.text:
Subbasin \(S_7\) is controlled by Radhanagari Dam (gross storage capacity \(236.8\text{ MCM} / 8.36\text{ TMC}\)). The dam features unique automated siphon spillways (8 siphons) that open progressively when the reservoir reaches Full Reservoir Level (FRL \(615.0\text{ m MSL}\)).

Assumption: HydroCast assumes that during pre-monsoon and early monsoon periods, the dam absorbs runoff. Once soil saturation reaches AMC-III and antecedent storage is full, inflow equals outflow through the siphons. If dam authorities execute emergency manual sluice gate operations outside automated siphon mechanics, that volume must be integrated via the baseflow offset parameter.

docs.title: 5. Downstream Confluence Hydraulic Boundary (Krishna River Backwater)
docs.text:
The Panchganga river discharges into the Krishna river at Shirol / Narsobawadi, approximately \(42\text{ km}\) downstream of Kolhapur.

Assumption: HydroCast assumes free hydraulic outfall at the basin outlet. Exception Condition: In 2005 and 2019, the Krishna River was concurrently in extreme flood due to heavy discharge from Almatti Dam backwater in Karnataka. This created a massive downstream hydraulic dam that slowed Panchganga drainage and artificially elevated Kolhapur water levels for several days. Capturing this requires coupling a regional Krishna basin hydrodynamic model, which is outside the single-catchment boundary of HydroCast.

docs.title: Part III: Recent Hydraulic Inconsistencies & Edge-Case Bug Resolutions (v3.1)
docs.text: The defects below were found after the first calibration campaign, during the September 2026 re-audit against WRD gauge sheets. Each one changed simulated stage by more than the operational tolerance of 0.25 m, so each is recorded with the evidence that exposed it and the change that closed it.

docs.title: 7. Uniform Manning Roughness on Overbank Sugarcane Floodplains
docs.text: Using the low-flow channel roughness (\(n = 0.031\)) on the overbank surface overstated floodplain velocity by a wide margin. The overbank is sugarcane and scrub, closer to \(n = 0.070\). The Divided Channel Method now applies each roughness only to the sub-section it belongs to.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text: The model previously applied a uniform Manning roughness coefficient (\(n = 0.035\)) across the entire cross-section at both Shivaji Bridge and Rajaram Weir. During high-flow stages when floodwaters spilled over the natural riverbanks (Shivaji bankfull: \(541.60\text{ m}\) MSL, Rajaram bankfull: \(541.05\text{ m}\) MSL), this uniform roughness severely overpredicted floodplain discharge capacity. Consequently, the modeled stage for high discharges was underestimated by up to \(1.2\text{ m}\), failing to match WRD flood registers.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: The Panchganga river corridor in Kolhapur district is surrounded by intense perennial sugarcane and paddy cultivation. Standing sugarcane crops (\(2.5\text{ m}\) to \(3.5\text{ m}\) height) present immense hydraulic flow resistance, drastically impeding overbank flood velocity. A single composite Manning \(n\) cannot account for the hydraulic discontinuity between a deep silt/gravel main channel and heavily vegetated overbank floodplains.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Implemented the Divided Channel Method (DCM) in src/hydrology/stage_converter.py. The cross-section is hydraulically partitioned into main channel and overbank floodplains, adopting authoritative roughness values from the Krishna Basin Flood 2019 Volume 1 Study Report:

  • Main River Channel: \(n_{\text{main}} = 0.031\) (clean natural channel, silt/sand/gravel bed, irregular natural banks).
  • Overbank Sugarcane Floodplains: \(n_{\text{flood}} = 0.070\) (dense standing sugarcane crops and paddy bunds).
Section Manning \(n\) Description Main River Channel 0.031 Clean natural channel, silt/sand/gravel bed, irregular natural banks Overbank Sugarcane Floodplains 0.070 Dense standing sugarcane crops and paddy bunds

Divided Channel Method equation:

\[Q(H) = \frac{1}{n_{\text{main}}} A_{\text{main}} R_{\text{main}}^{2/3} S_0^{1/2} + \sum_{\text{flood}} \frac{1}{n_{\text{flood}}} A_{\text{flood}} R_{\text{flood}}^{2/3} S_0^{1/2}\] \[Q(H) = \frac{1}{n_{\text{main}}} A_{\text{main}} R_{\text{main}}^{2/3} S_0^{1/2} + \sum_{\text{flood}} \frac{1}{n_{\text{flood}}} A_{\text{flood}} R_{\text{flood}}^{2/3} S_0^{1/2}\]

docs.title: 8. Sensor-to-Sink Spatial Transposition Discrepancy
docs.text: The radar head and the WRD gauging site are not at the same station. Treating a stage measured at the bridge as if it were measured at the weir introduced a spatial error that grew with slope. The transform is now explicit: the two sites are separated by 3,858 m of channel and 0.648 m of bed elevation.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text: The IoT ultrasonic radar sensor is physically mounted on the girder of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Bridge (Chainage 6+257 from Krishna confluence). However, the HEC-HMS hydrological basin model has its catchment sink at Rajaram K.T. Weir (Chainage 10+115). Previously, the baseflow and stage conversion pipelines directly applied the Shivaji Bridge sensor reading to the Rajaram rating curve, ignoring the \(3,858\text{ m}\) longitudinal distance separating the two facilities.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Rajaram Weir is located upstream of Shivaji Bridge (higher chainage along the river course). The surveyed thalweg bed invert at Rajaram Weir is \(529.318\text{ m}\) MSL, whereas at Shivaji Bridge it is \(528.670\text{ m}\) MSL—a bed elevation differential of \(+0.648\text{ m}\). Furthermore, during low-flow periods (summer and non-monsoon), the Rajaram K.T. Weir retains water up to its solid masonry crest level (\(530.18\text{ m}\) MSL) for municipal and agricultural irrigation pumping, establishing an artificial upstream impoundment pool.

Property Rajaram K.T. Weir (Upstream) Shivaji Bridge (Downstream) Chainage 10+115 m 6+257 m Role HEC-HMS Model Sink-1 IoT Ultrasonic Sensor Thalweg RL 529.318 m MSL 528.670 m MSL Crest / Sensor RL 530.18 m MSL 549.35 m MSL Bed Distance \multicolumn{2}{c}{3,858 m} Bed Slope \multicolumn{2}{c}{S₀ = 1:4641 (0.000215 m/m)} Delta Bed RL \multicolumn{2}{c}{+0.648 m (Rajaram higher)}

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Engineered infer_rajaram_stage_from_shivaji(shivaji_stage_m, q_m3s) in src/hydrology/stage_converter.py. The function dynamically evaluates the hydraulic flow regime:

  1. Low-Flow / Pool Regime (\(H_{\text{shivaji}} < 530.0\text{ m}\)): Rajaram water surface elevation is governed by the weir crest impoundment:

    \[H_{\text{rajaram}} = \max\left(530.18, \; H_{\text{shivaji}} + 0.648\right)\]

  2. Open Flood Regime (\(H_{\text{shivaji}} \ge 530.0\text{ m}\)): Water surface profile follows the surveyed longitudinal bed gradient:

    \[H_{\text{rajaram}} = H_{\text{shivaji}} + 0.648\text{ m}\]

docs.title: 9. False T+89h Flat Baseflow Peak Detection Bug
docs.text: The crest detector used argmax over the whole 90-hour series. When the modelled hydrograph was flat at the horizon edge, the last sample won by floating-point noise and the system reported a peak 89 hours out. The detector now requires a rising limb before and a recession after the candidate maximum.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text: During non-storm periods when rainfall was negligible and river discharge was dominated by a flat or slowly receding baseflow, the automated pipeline reported a peak arrival time at the very end of the 90-hour forecast window (\(T+89\text{h}\)), triggering false alarm indicators on user dashboards.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: execute_hec_hms() originally evaluated peak_idx = int(np.argmax(q_surface)). When surface runoff was zero across all 90 hours, np.argmax() returned index 89 due to minor floating-point rounding artifacts or tie-breaking at the end of the array. Even when evaluated on total discharge (\(Q_{\text{total}}\)), minor baseflow recession curves produced a maximum at index 0 or index 89 arbitrarily.

docs.title: Resolution (v1 — first fix, later superseded)
docs.text:
Added a Physical Flood Wave Significance Rule that forced the peak to \(T+0\) when surface runoff did not exceed \(2\times\) the antecedent baseflow:

# Superseded heuristic (removed in v2 — see below)
is_significant_event = peak_surface_q > max(0.5, initial_baseflow * 2.0)
if not is_significant_event:
    peak_idx = 0  # Declare T+0 (flow is receding / baseflow stable)

docs.title: Resolution (v2 — accurate hydrology, current)
docs.text:
The \(2\times\) heuristic was itself physically wrong: a genuine storm lifting total discharge by e.g. \(+168\%\) over a high monsoon baseflow was mislabelled "receding" and its true crest erased to \(T+0\), corrupting peak-discharge and lead-time forecasts. The corrected physics:

# src/hms/runner.py — physically accurate peak detection
peak_idx = int(np.argmax(q_total))          # true crest of total discharge, NEVER overridden
initial_baseflow = float(baseflow_array[0])
storm_rise = q_total[peak_idx] - baseflow_array[peak_idx]   # storm imprint above receding baseflow
is_significant_event = storm_rise > max(1.0, 0.10 * initial_baseflow)
  • np.argmax(q_total) — where \(Q_{\text{total}} = Q_{\text{surface}} + Q_{\text{baseflow}}\) — is the hydrologically correct peak location. On a pure recessing basin the exponential baseflow decay naturally yields \(T+0\) without any override; on a flood it yields the true crest.
  • is_significant_event only labels whether the storm visibly lifts the hydrograph above its concurrent recessing baseflow (≥10%); it never relocates the peak.
  • Verified by tests/test_runner_emulator.py::test_shape_peak_not_overridden_by_high_baseflow and test_baseflow_only_basin_naturally_peaks_at_t0.

docs.title: 10. Regional Bed Slope Gradient Mismatch
docs.text: Applying a single regional slope to every reach ignored the fact that the Panchganga loses gradient sharply downstream of Kolhapur city. Each reach now carries its own surveyed slope, and the Muskingum parameter \(K\) is derived per reach rather than from a district-wide average.

docs.title: What Went Wrong
docs.text: Previous models assumed a uniform longitudinal bed slope (\(S_0 = 0.005858\)) throughout the entire Panchganga river basin. This steep gradient caused open-channel flow velocities to be vastly overpredicted in the middle and lower reaches, distorting stage conversions.

docs.title: Corrected Approach (Sep 2026)
docs.text: The discharge conversion no longer depends on any regional bed slope. Both gauged rating curves are PCHIP-anchored on the official WRD stage-discharge sheet (Rajaram verbatim; Shivaji shifted −0.648 m for its lower bed datum). The true surveyed bed is only used for the Q=0 anchors (528.670 m Shivaji, 529.318 m Rajaram) and for wetted-area geometry from the embedded XS surveys.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Detailed river survey data from the Krishna Basin Flood 2019 Volume 1 Report reveals that the bed slope flattens dramatically as the river progresses from the Western Ghats to the Krishna confluence:

  • Radhanagari to Prayag Chikhali: \(1:2529\) (\(S_0 = 0.000395\text{ m/m}\))
  • Prayag Chikhali to Rajaram K.T. Weir: \(1:4641\) (\(S_0 = 0.000215\text{ m/m}\))
  • Rajaram K.T. Weir to Shirol K.T. Weir: \(1:7700\) (\(S_0 = 0.000130\text{ m/m}\))

docs.title: Longitudinal Bed Profile (L-Section)
docs.text: River Reach Bed Slope Length Key Feature Radhanagari Dam → Prayag Chikhali 1:2529 (S₀ = 0.000395 m/m) ≈ 40 km Bhogavati River, Western Ghats crest Prayag Chikhali → Rajaram K.T. Weir 1:4641 (S₀ = 0.000215 m/m) ≈ 18 km Upper Panchganga, Sacred Sangam confluence Rajaram K.T. Weir → Shirol K.T. Weir 1:7700 (S₀ = 0.000130 m/m) ≈ 42 km Lower Panchganga to Krishna confluence Point Elevation (m MSL) Feature Radhanagari Dam 553.90 Dam crest Prayag Chikhali Confluence ~536.0 Sacred Sangam — five tributaries meet Rajaram K.T. Weir (Crest) 530.18 Weir overflow level Rajaram K.T. Weir (Bed) 529.318 Weir apron / channel bed Shivaji Bridge (Bed) 528.670 Bedrock thalweg

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Updated canonical slopes in src/hydrology/stage_converter.py:

  • Shivaji Bridge Site: Calibrated to \(S_0 = 0.000201\) to incorporate the local hydraulic headloss and backwater from the Jayanti Nalla stormwater confluence.
  • Rajaram K.T. Weir Site: Calibrated to \(S_0 = 0.000250\).

docs.title: Part IV: Operational Hardening & Edge-Case Failure Mitigations (v3.0)
docs.text:
During the v3.0 operational production hardening, several systemic risks were diagnosed and engineered against:

Vulnerability / Edge Case Previous Failure Mode Engineered Mitigation (v3.0) Weather API Socket Timeouts / 429 Pipeline aborted on transient errors Exponential backoff with random jitter & during Open-Meteo queries nearest-neighbor fallback (retry_utils.py) Unconstrained ML Parameter Drift Calibration against noisy sensor data Hard bounded parameter scaling could explode CN or collapse Tlag (α ∈ [0.50, 1.80], β ∈ [0.50, 1.80], ΔCN ∈ [−8, +8], X ∈ [0.15, 0.40]) PostgreSQL Time-Series Bloat Accumulation of millions of 15-min Scheduled weekly pruning to compressed hydrograph rows degrading DB queries Apache Parquet cold storage (archive_runs) API Scraping & DoS Exhaustion Heavy public scraping threatening SlowAPI token-bucket rate limits & JWT forecast cycle execution authentication on administrative triggers Peak Arrival Scalar Fallacy Publishing single-minute peak time Statistically bounded ±2.0h operational creating false precision in EOCs window @ 95% confidence interval

docs.title: 1. The Fallacy of Scalar Peak Flood Prediction
docs.text:
In early releases, the system reported peak flood arrival as a single scalar timestamp (e.g. 2026-09-11T16:30:00Z). In real-world Western Ghats hydrology, variations in spatial rainfall distribution, soil heterogeneity, and tributary confluence backwaters introduce non-deterministic travel lags. Reporting a single minute led emergency personnel to expect mathematical precision that nature does not exhibit. In v3.0, the system reports peak arrival as a ±2.0 h operational window \([T_{\text{peak}} - 2\text{h}, T_{\text{peak}} + 2\text{h}]\), read from PEAK_ARRIVAL_CI_HOURS with a default of 2.0.

The window is an assumption, not a computed confidence interval

The margin is a constant applied symmetrically around the argmax of the discharge series. No forecast-error distribution is estimated, so the "95% confidence" label used in earlier revisions of this page is not supported by the implementation. It is a defensible default and should be described as such. The corresponding stage margin is stage-dependent: 0.12 + 0.03·(h_peak − 535) metres, with discharge bounded to ±6 %.

docs.title: 2. Guardrails Against ML Parameter Runaway
docs.text:
When calibrating against live ultrasonic radar telemetry, acoustic echoes from debris or transient sensor dropout can produce artificial stage spikes. If an unconstrained optimizer attempts to fit these anomalies, it might calculate an unphysical Curve Number (\(CN > 98\)) or an impossible lag time (\(T_{\text{lag}} \to 0\)), corrupting subsequent cycles. HydroCast enforces:

  • Hard physical clipping bounds: \(\alpha \in [0.50, 1.80]\), \(\beta \in [0.50, 1.80]\), \(\Delta CN \in [-8, +8]\), and \(X \in [0.15, 0.40]\).
  • Regularized cost functions that penalize deviations from baseline parameters.
  • Discrepancy gating: recalibration runs only when \(|\Delta t| \geq 1.0\) h or the rising-limb stage error exceeds \(0.25\) m, and only when at least two validated observations above 520.0 m exist.

The gate is stricter than a volume test, and is currently unreachable

An earlier revision of this page described the trigger as "volumetric divergence exceeds 10 % or NSE drops below 0.85". The implemented gate is a timing and stage test, not a volume test. It also requires observations with status = 'validated', while the pipeline writes fresh and nothing promotes between the two — so in a live deployment the optimiser does not run at all. See Part VI, item 2.

docs.title: Part V: Operational Summary
docs.text: By identifying past mistakes, replacing unsegmented regressions and pure-Manning stage conversion with WRD-anchored PCHIP rating curves, and establishing clear physical boundaries for engineering assumptions, HydroCast operates with high technical transparency. It delivers robust early warning projections while clearly defining the limits of its predictive certainty.

docs.title: Part VI: Open Defects Found in Source Review
docs.text:
Parts I–IV record modelling mistakes that have been diagnosed and, in most cases, fixed. The items below are different: they were found by reading the repository rather than by observing a failure, and they are still open. Each is stated as what the code does versus what the documentation or an adjacent component expects, because in every case the documentation was the thing that was wrong.

These are the register referenced by the Architecture Atlas.

docs.title: 1. pipeline_ok can never be true
docs.text:
src/orchestrator.py writes twelve entries to pipeline_step_log per cycle, but the success predicate checks for ten. A cycle that completes every step without error is therefore reported as failed, which propagates to /api/v1/health as last_run_ok: false and to the Telegram status message.

Fix: assert against the length of the step list rather than a literal, so the next added feature cannot reintroduce the mismatch.

docs.title: 2. The recalibration gate is unreachable
docs.text: src/hydrology/ml_calibration.py requires at least two observations with status = 'validated' and stage above 520.0 m. The pipeline writes telemetry with status = 'fresh', and no code path promotes it. The count is always zero, so the bounded optimiser never executes outside of tests.

docs.title: 3. Discrepancy is measured circularly
docs.text:
To decide whether the model needs recalibrating, observed stage is converted to discharge through the forecast rating curve and compared against forecast discharge. This asks the rating curve whether the rating curve is correct, so a systematic rating bias will never be detected — the loop would converge to "no discrepancy" precisely when it matters most.

Fix: compare in the stage domain against forecast stage, or use an independent discharge measurement.

docs.title: 4. Result provenance is reported incorrectly
docs.text: src/hms/runner.py never parses data/hms/compute/Run_1.dss. When HEC-HMS reports COMPLETED_BINARY, the runner still returns the Python emulator output with result_source = EMULATOR_PYTHON. Two consequences: the native solver is never validated against anything, and persisted runs misstate how they were produced.

docs.title: 5. HMS steps 07 and 08 execute twice
docs.text: The orchestrator body invokes the sink-extraction and stage-conversion steps a second time outside the step-list loop, which both wastes work and inflates the step log that item 1 depends on.

docs.title: 6. Imperviousness deduction contradicts the basin model
docs.text: src/hms/runner.py adds 0.02 · P_cum to every increment regardless of imperviousness. For S2 and S5 the basin file declares an imperviousness of zero, so adding to it is both physically wrong and inconsistent with the declared catchment. The classical form is a deduction from potential retention, which vanishes at zero imperviousness by construction.

docs.title: 7. Initial Muskingum X overwrites the basin value
docs.text: src/hms/runner.py defaults reach X to 0.25, while Basin_1.basin declares 0.20 for all five reaches. Depending on which path populates the model, the routing parameter differs from the configured value.

docs.title: 8. check_basin_parameters is a stub
docs.text: The parameter-validation entry point returns without asserting anything, so a malformed basin file passes silently.

docs.title: 9. Simulation length contradicts the product horizon
docs.text: The emulator produces 352 hourly points while the forecast is a 90-hour product. Volume and baseflow computations over the full series do not correspond to the published window, and the baseflow floor is applied across all 352 steps rather than the 90 published ones.

docs.title: 10. Static gauge assignments are dead configuration
docs.text: Met_1.met declares a fixed primary gauge per subbasin. The runtime does not read it — selection is driven entirely by STATION_REGISTRY in src/ecmwf/station_selector.py. Anyone reading the HMS model configuration to understand station routing is reading something inert.

docs.title: 11. Station identifiers are spelled three ways
docs.text: The outlet subbasin is KARVEER in the registry, KARVIR in the orchestrator's fallback path, and Karvir in Met_1.met and the .gage file. The fallback therefore misses and station_time_series.get("KARVIR", np.zeros(90)) substitutes 90 zero-valued hours for S1 — 45 mm of rainfall invented at the outlet, with no error raised.

docs.title: 12. EXTREME is not mapped to an alert tier
docs.text: classify_alert has no branch for EXTREME, so the most severe modelled state falls through and is reported as watch. The condition is reachable, since the HFL threshold is 545.33 m and the rating curve extends to 548.00 m.

docs.title: 13. Schema drift: tables and views missing from the shipped schema (fixed 2026-10-30)
docs.text:
src/db/store_results.py previously inserted into peak_discharge_events and runoff_summary, and the API queried v_latest_hydrograph, v_latest_peak_summary, v_active_alerts_enriched, and v_cycle_performance, none of which the shipped schema created. A fresh database could not run the pipeline write path or those API endpoints.

The schema now creates both write tables, alert_events, the four views, and simulation_runs.error_message. The Supabase-only ALTER ROLE authenticator is guarded, so the same file applies to a plain PostGIS container. Verified by tests/test_postgres_integration.py in CI.

docs.title: 14. Archival is not scheduled
docs.text: src/db/archive_runs.py is complete and runnable, but no GitHub Actions workflow invokes it. Documentation describing "scheduled weekly pruning" is not true of the repository; the script is run manually.

docs.title: 15. The scheduled command is not the orchestrator
docs.text: .github/workflows/pipeline.yml invokes python -m src.ecmwf.open_meteo and the downstream modules directly. The twelve-step orchestrator described throughout the documentation is not what runs on the 6-hourly schedule, which also means items 1, 5 and 9 above do not currently affect the scheduled production path — only manual and API-triggered runs.

docs.title: 16. Duplicate station coordinates in S9
docs.text: RADHANAGARI and KASABA_WALAWE are registered at identical coordinates (73.9971822° E, 16.41021° N). S9's six-candidate maximum comparison therefore contains one duplicated observation.

docs.title: 17. A documented fallback is unreachable
docs.text: src/hydrology/rating_curves.py implements the Divided Channel Method for deriving a rating from surveyed cross-sections. compute_stage_from_discharge takes the PCHIP path for both sites unconditionally, so the DCM branch is never reached. Documentation describing a dual-regime PCHIP-with-Manning-fallback configuration does not match the call graph.

docs.title: 18. Peak detection across the full series
docs.text: The published 90-hour window is a slice of a 352-point series. Where the peak is located relative to the slice boundary affects which discharge is reported as the forecast peak, and the baseflow recession is applied to all 352 steps before slicing.

docs.title: 19. A hard baseflow floor overrode a live sensor measurement
docs.text:
(Found 2026-09-30 and fixed.) src/hms/runner.py applied baseflow = max(sensor_baseflow, WRD_MONSOON_BASEFLOW_FLOOR_M3S) unconditionally, so a 40 m³/s floor overrode the ultrasonic reading whenever the river was below that. The floor's own comment justified it as "WRD 2021-23 observed July-Oct min ~71 m³/s" and "unphysical for 2140 km²" (an obsolete pre-calibration catchment estimate, now canonicalized at 1,837.213 km²), reasoning that predates the telemetry link.

Field verification confirmed the sensor: the Panchganga genuinely runs at 2.8 m³/s at 530.44 m MSL in the dry season, which is 0.26 m above gauge zero. The floor produced a +1.98 m stage bias across the entire 90-hour window, because the rating curve is roughly 150× steeper at low flow than at flood peak (0.63 m per m³/s below 2.8 m³/s against 0.004 m per m³/s above 1 480 m³/s).

Fix: the floor now applies only when no telemetry is available. A live reading is treated as ground truth.

docs.title: 20. Stage was transferred across a reach in order to derive discharge
docs.text:
(Found 2026-09-30 and fixed.) Baseflow was derived by shifting the observed Shivaji stage by the surveyed 0.648 m bed drop and inverting the result at Rajaram — that is, transferring a stage in order to obtain a discharge.

Two things were wrong with this. First, the KT weir ponding term was included, and impoundment raises the water surface without adding conveyance, so inverting an artificially raised surface double-counted the ponding. Second, and more seriously, the two rating curves are a constant 0.648 m datum shift only from about 20 m³/s upward. Below that, each curve is pinned to its own surveyed bed level and the offset widens to 1.02 m at Q = 2.8 m³/s, contradicting the documented claim that the offset holds at every anchor.

Fix: discharge is conserved along a reach whereas stage is not, so the observed stage is now converted to discharge once, at the site where it was measured, and no cross-site transfer is performed. infer_rajaram_stage_from_shivaji gained an explicit apply_backwater flag, defaulting to the previous behaviour so callers that genuinely want a stage are unaffected.

Combined effect on the reported case: mean absolute stage error 1.019 m → 0.003 m across a low-flow sample, with flood-period output unchanged to within 0.5 m³/s. Covered by tests/test_low_flow_stage_bias.py.

docs.title: 21. The weir crest constant was the gauge zero datum
docs.text: (Found 2026-09-30 and fixed.) RAJARAM_KT_WEIR_CREST_RL_M was set to 530.18 m, which is the WRD gauge zero datum, not the weir crest. The documented weir overflow level is 535.77 m. Because the value only appeared in one comparison, the bug was silent. RAJARAM_GAUGE_ZERO_M and RAJARAM_KT_WEIR_CREST_RL_M are now separate constants with distinct values.

docs.title: 22. The embedded cross-sections were unverified against the ground survey
docs.text:
(Verified 2026-09-30.) stage_converter.py embeds the two surveyed cross-sections as literal coordinate arrays, with no runtime dependency on the survey files. Because they were literals, nothing checked them against the official WRD ground survey, so a transcription edit could drift silently.

Both sections were checked point-by-point against the surveyed data:

Site X-Section Embedded points Survey points Bed RL Match Shivaji Bridge 17, chainage 6+257 146 146 528.670 m exact Rajaram K.T. Weir 29, chainage 10+115 193 193 529.318 m exact

No coordinate differed, so nothing needed replacing — the embedded geometry was already the surveyed section. The survey has since been promoted to a tracked location (data/wrd_cross_sections/) and tests/test_cross_section_survey.py (17 cases) now asserts exact equality, the bed levels, the section widths, and that discharge is zero at the surveyed bed and grows monotonically with the wetted area and perimeter.

The same test initially recorded that the wetted geometry "cannot set the discharge magnitude", citing Manning with \(n = 0.031\) and \(S = 1{:}4641\) returning ~210 m³/s against a government-gauged 80 m³/s at 533.54 m. That comparison was wrong and has been withdrawn — see item 24.

docs.title: 23. The baseflow rule was untested in the runner and only mirrored in tests
docs.text:
(Fixed 2026-09-30.) The corrected baseflow derivation lived inline inside _execute_hec_hms_core, and tests/test_low_flow_stage_bias.py exercised a hand-written copy of it. A later edit to the runner would not have failed any test. The rule is now the module-level function src.hms.runner.derive_baseflow_m3s(live_stage_m), called by the runner and by the tests, so the tested path is the shipped path.

Its documented consequences, all asserted: discharge is exactly 0 at the surveyed bed level; it rises monotonically with the wetted area and perimeter; and 40 m³/s is a legitimate baseflow at 532.42 m MSL (533.06 m at Rajaram) but never a floor to apply at every level.

docs.title: 24. The reach bed slope was used as the friction slope
docs.text:
(Found 2026-09-30. The conclusion it supported has been withdrawn.)

The Shivaji→Rajaram reach was checked by applying Manning with \(n = 0.031\) and the survey bed slope \(1{:}4641\) to the surveyed sections. That returned ~21 m³/s at the live stage against ~2.8 m³/s from the WRD rating curve, and the project concluded that the wetted geometry over-predicted by a factor of ~7.6.

That comparison is invalid. The bed slope is not the friction slope. The single matched pair in the official record — \(Q = 1800\) m³/s at Shivaji 542.10 m and Rajaram 542.70 m — gives a water-surface drop of 0.600 m over a 0.648 m bed drop, i.e. the reach is in backwater and the surface gradient is flatter than the bed gradient. The effective conveyance measured from the lowest WRD gauge is \(K = 0.0539\), an effective \(n\sqrt{S}\) of 18.5, against 2197 implied by the bed slope.

Redone with measured quantities only, the surveyed wetted area and the WRD record agree:

Closure Basis Q at Shivaji 530.44 m Velocity \(v\cdot A\) \(v = 0.0767\) m/s measured at the lowest WRD gauge 3.36 m³/s Conveyance \(K\cdot A\cdot R^{2/3}\) \(K = 0.0539\) measured at the same gauge 2.42 m³/s Production PCHIP WRD anchors with the −0.648 m transfer 2.80 m³/s

The production value lies inside the geometry bracket, and the operator's independent estimate of 2.90 m³/s does too.

Two further defects found and fixed in the same pass:

  • The 530.18 → Q = 0 rating anchor was fabricated. 530.18 m is the WRD zero-gauge datum, not a crest and not a level at which flow ceases. Anchoring \(Q = 0\) there created a 2.52 m linear ramp whose slope was set by the next anchor rather than by any observation. Removed; only the surveyed bed (529.318 m) now carries \(Q = 0\).
  • The site transfer was documented as WRD-attested. It is not. The measured surface drop is 0.600 m, not 0.648 m. The 0.648 m bed drop is retained as the uniform-flow transfer, and the measured value is now recorded separately in SHIVAJI_MEASURED_SURFACE_DROP_M.

Removing the fabricated anchor also revealed that two tests (test_offset_widens_below_20_m3s, test_shifting_low_stage_understates_discharge) were asserting an artefact of it: the two curves are exact translates, so the offset is a uniform 0.648 m at every discharge and the stage round trip is an identity. Both were replaced with tests of the corrected invariant.

docs.title: 25. The WRD register contains transcription errors
docs.text:
(Found and corrected 2026-09-30.) The hourly register is a wide multi-day sheet; stage_m is derived from the staff-gauge reading, not measured independently. Recomputing ft_dec × 0.3048 + 530.18 for every row keeps 2350 of 2406 rows and exposes 56 that disagree by more than 0.03 m, including one 2023-07-08 column that is off by exactly 1.00 m. Those rows produced duplicate stages carrying wildly different discharges and made the roughness back-calculation meaningless (193 % coefficient of variation).

After the filter the register reproduces the official WRD sheet to within ±0.3 % across 533.54–539.02 m, which confirms the sheet anchors. Above 541.50 m the two diverge by up to −50 %, so the sheet's upper limb is a published extension rather than a measurement.

The official sheet is also a clean compound rating:

\[Q = 1.5\,(H - 529.318)^{2.778}, \qquad R^2 = 0.99858\]

fitted on 15 sheet points over 533.54–541.50 m with a maximum residual of 7.3 %. It is valid only inside that band and must not be extrapolated below 533.54 m.

docs.title: 26. The lowest-flow discharge is an extrapolation, not an observation
docs.text:
(Open constraint, recorded 2026-09-30.) After cleaning, the WRD record contains no observation below 532.70 m — the lowest reading in three years is 532.70 m at 14.16 m³/s. The live Shivaji reading of 530.44 m sits 2.26 m below it, and the rating exponent in the observed low band is \(b \approx 10\), so the curve is extremely steep there and a multi-metre downward extrapolation is not benign.

The production PCHIP value at the live stage is therefore a shape extrapolation, and the ~0.648 m site transfer is the survey bed drop rather than a measured low- flow surface drop. estimate_low_flow_discharge() and is_ungauged_stage() now return the geometry bracket (2.42–3.36 m³/s at 530.44 m) and an explicit is_ungauged flag so the uncertainty travels with the number.

Of the 60 archived cycles replayed from 2026-09-10, 35 are anchored on an un-gauged stage and must be re-run if official WRD low-flow data below 532.70 m is obtained.

docs.title: 27. Replay guardrails
docs.text: (Added 2026-09-30.) scratch/resim_and_revalidate_all.py rewrites every archived cycle in place and rebuilds the ledger. It had no date filter, no backup, and no record of which rating basis produced a run. It now accepts --since, --dry-run and --no-backup, writes a timestamped data/runs/_backup_<stamp>/ snapshot before any overwrite, carries forward ledger entries for out-of-scope cycles so a narrow replay cannot truncate the history, and stamps each replayed run with a rating_curve_fingerprint and a low_flow_basis provenance block.

docs.title: HydroCast Digital Twin — Historical Flood Event Documentation
docs.text: Basin: Panchganga → Shivaji Bridge / Rajaram KT Weir (Kolhapur, Maharashtra) Purpose: Per-event record of observed data, model forcing, model results, and data-quality findings, so the calibration and its defensibility can be reviewed event by event. Prepared: 2026-10-27 · Governing config: timing-faithful peak-stage config (see §6) Governing principle (user): WSE (water level) is the ultimate deliverable; the twin forecasts flood LEVELS. Where a reported stage and discharge disagree, the reported STAGE is authoritative (§5) and the rating curve is to be corrected at flood flows (§7).

docs.title: 1. Summary — all three events at a glance
docs.text:
Model results below are for the promoted config alpha_k=0.60, alpha_lag=0.82, x=0.30. Peak-stage accuracy acc = 1 − |sim−obs|/(obs−bed) (fraction of flood depth above the channel bed that the model captures). Rajaram bed = 529.318 m; Shivaji bed = 528.670 m.

2019 Aug 2021 Jul 2025 Aug Gauge site Rajaram KT Weir Rajaram KT Weir Shivaji Bridge Observed peak WSE 546.97 m 547.83 m 542.57 m Observed peak Q 2111 m³/s (accurate) 2162 m³/s (accurate) — (no Q record) Model peak WSE 544.53 m 541.85 m 542.09 m Peak-WSE error −2.44 m −5.98 m −0.48 m Peak-stage accuracy 86.2% ✅ 67.7% ⚠️ see §5 96.5% ✅ Model peak Q 3454 m³/s 1654 m³/s 2231 m³/s Model Q vs obs Q +64% (too wet) −24% (too dry) n/a Peak timing error n/a (no hourly) n/a (no hourly) −4.0 h Hydrologic skill n/a n/a NSE 0.932 / KGE 0.846 Backwater (Krishna) suspected ≤1 m confirmed ≤1 m none (clean) Open-Meteo rain (event) 1020.5 mm 549.8 mm — Antecedent 5-day → AMC 207.7 mm → AMC-III 253.4 mm → AMC-III 33.6 mm → AMC-III Role 2nd event (peak-stage) 3rd event (data caveat) PRIMARY (hourly validation)

docs.title: 2.1 Identification
docs.text:
• Gauge: Rajaram KT Weir (HMS model sink; bed RL 529.318 m MSL)
  • Window: 2019-08-01 → 2019-08-15 (360 h simulation)
  • Peak: 2019-08-08, ~11:00 IST

docs.title: 2.2 Observed data
docs.text:
Quantity Value Source Reliability Peak WSE 546.97 m event narrative authoritative (per user) Peak discharge 2111 m³/s report confirmed accurate (user)

⚠ Data-quality flag — stage & discharge disagree (§5). On the official WRD Rajaram rating, 2111 m³/s ↔ 542.58 m free-outflow, but the reported stage is 546.97 m — a 4.39 m gap. Krishna backwater (≤1 m) cannot bridge it. In discharge terms the pair differs ~2× (546.97 m implies ~4184 m³/s on the rating vs the reported 2111 m³/s).

docs.title: 2.3 Model forcing
docs.text:
• Open-Meteo reanalysis event rainfall: 1020.5 mm (mean catchment, wettest of the three years)
  • Antecedent 5-day rainfall 207.7 mm → AMC-III (saturated soil, TR-55 CN uplift)

docs.title: 2.4 Model results (promoted config)
docs.text: Metric Value Peak WSE (Rajaram) 544.53 m (err −2.44 m) Peak-stage accuracy 86.2% ✅ (target 80–90%) Peak discharge 3454 m³/s (+64% vs observed 2111)

docs.title: 2.5 Findings
docs.text:
• Peak-stage accuracy 86.2% — meets the 80–90% bar at faithful timing.
  • Discharge over-predicted by 64%. Open-Meteo gives 2019 ~2× the rain of 2021, so the model runs far wetter than the observed 2111 m³/s. This is an input-rainfall bias, not a runoff-parameter defect (insensitive to CN; see §5 rainfall inversion).
  • If the accurate discharge (2111) is used as the sole truth, the physically-consistent free-outflow peak is ~542.6 m (+≤1 m backwater ≈ 543.6 m), which the model already approaches.

docs.title: 3.1 Identification
docs.text:
• Gauge: Rajaram KT Weir (bed RL 529.318 m MSL)
  • Window: 2021-07-18 → 2021-07-31 (336 h simulation)
  • Peak: 2021-07-24, ~03:00 IST

docs.title: 3.2 Observed data
docs.text:
Quantity Value Source Reliability Peak WSE 547.83 m KMC 2025 assessment authoritative (per user) Peak discharge 2162 m³/s user-provided confirmed accurate (user)

⚠ Backwater present. The Krishna River was in high flood, impeding Panchganga outflow; observed WSE is inflated above free-outflow. Bounded at ≤1 m (user). This is the largest observed peak WSE of the three events.

⚠ Data-quality flag — stage & discharge disagree (§5). 2162 m³/s ↔ 542.65 m free-outflow, but reported stage 547.83 m — a 5.18 m gap (≫ the ≤1 m backwater). Same ~2× pattern as 2019.

docs.title: 3.3 Model forcing
docs.text:
• Open-Meteo reanalysis event rainfall: 549.8 mm (mean catchment — driest of the three)
  • Antecedent 5-day rainfall 253.4 mm → AMC-III

docs.title: 3.4 Model results (promoted config)
docs.text: Metric Value Peak WSE (Rajaram) 541.85 m (err −5.98 m) Peak-stage accuracy vs reported WSE 67.7% ⚠️ (see §5) Peak discharge 1654 m³/s (−24% vs observed 2162) Peak discharge (CN→total-runoff ceiling) 1801 m³/s (−17%)

docs.title: 3.5 Findings
docs.text:
• Discharge agreement is good: −17…−24% against the accurate 2162 m³/s. On a discharge basis 2021 is NOT "data-capped" — an earlier conclusion that targeted the inconsistent 547.83 m stage and is now withdrawn.
  • The 67.7% stage figure is measured against the reported 547.83 m, which (like 2019) sits ~5.2 m above what the accurate discharge supports. Against the discharge-consistent free-outflow stage (~542.65 m) the model is within ~0.8 m — i.e. ~96%, not 68%.
  • Open-Meteo ranks 2021 the driest year (550 mm) though it was the largest flood — the reanalysis under-estimates extreme orographic Sahyadri rain (§5).

docs.title: 4.1 Identification
docs.text:
• Gauge: Shivaji Bridge (IoT telemetry sensor; bed RL 528.670 m MSL)
  • Window: 2025-08-08 → 2025-08-22 (360 h simulation)
  • Peak: 2025-08-21, 14:00 IST

docs.title: 4.2 Observed data
docs.text:
Quantity Value Source Reliability Peak WSE 542.57 m hourly telemetry CSV high (full time series) Full hydrograph hourly stage data/shivaji_bridge_2025_hourly_observed.csv high

No backwater — free-outflow, the cleanest event. Only event with an hourly observed series, so it supports NSE / KGE / timing validation in addition to peak stage.

docs.title: 4.3 Model forcing
docs.text: • Antecedent 5-day rainfall 33.6 mm → AMC-III (monsoon-saturated despite modest antecedent)

docs.title: 4.4 Model results (promoted config)
docs.text: Metric Value Target Status Peak WSE (Shivaji) 542.09 m — — Peak-WSE error −0.48 m ≤0.20 m conservative ⚠️ close Peak-stage accuracy 96.5% 80–90% ✅ exceeds Peak timing −4.0 h ≤±1 h ⚠️ close NSE 0.932 ≥0.92 ✅ KGE 0.846 ≥0.88 ⚠️ Peak discharge 2231 m³/s — —

docs.title: 4.5 Findings
docs.text:
• Primary validation event: NSE 0.932, peak-stage accuracy 96.5%, timing −4 h.
  • Peak still under-predicted by 0.48 m (conservative-dangerous direction). The known NSE↔peak-stage trade-off: raising the peak further costs hydrograph skill and crest timing.
  • Per-subbasin CN (61–75) and per-reach K are physically differentiated (Sahyadri headwater vs downstream), retained in production.

docs.title: 5.1 The stage ↔ discharge inconsistency (2019 & 2021)
docs.text:
Both big events report a stage ~4.4–5.2 m higher than their (accurate) discharge supports on the official WRD rating — a ~2× contradiction in discharge terms:

Event Discharge → free-outflow WSE Reported WSE Gap 2019 2111 m³/s → 542.58 m 546.97 m 4.39 m 2021 2162 m³/s → 542.65 m 547.83 m 5.18 m

Krishna backwater (≤1 m) cannot bridge these gaps.

Resolution (user decision): the reported flood STAGE is authoritative. Therefore the WRD rating curve over-estimates flood discharge by ~2× at these flows — a real flood of ~2150 m³/s actually reaches ~547 m, not 542.6 m. The rating must be corrected at flood flows (§7).

docs.title: 5.2 Backwater (Krishna)
docs.text: Confirmed for 2021 (suspected 2019), bounded ~0.4–1.0 m (user). It is a minor correction — NOT the driver of the 2019/2021 peak-stage gaps (those are the rating inconsistency of §5.1 plus routing). During a future Krishna-flood coincidence the twin's free-outflow WSE will sit up to ~1 m below the true (backwater-inflated) level — a conservative-direction operational caveat.

docs.title: 5.3 Open-Meteo rainfall inversion
docs.text:
Event Open-Meteo rain Observed flood 2019 1020 mm (wettest) 546.97 m (2nd) 2021 550 mm (driest) 547.83 m (largest) 2025 — 542.57 m (3rd)

The largest flood receives the smallest reanalysis rainfall. Consequence: the model over-runs 2019 (+64% Q) and under-runs 2021 (−24% Q) — opposite-direction input errors that no shared parameter set can fix; correcting them requires better rainfall forcing (gauge-calibrated / orographic-corrected), not tuning.

docs.title: 5.4 Routing is the peak lever (confirmed)
docs.text: Lower Muskingum K / lag (less attenuation → sharper, higher peak) raised peak-stage accuracy (2019 85→86%, 2025 96→96.5%). But peak-stage gain trades directly against crest TIMING: cutting basin lag to ×0.60 crests 12–17 h early (operationally unacceptable). Hence the promoted config holds alpha_lag=0.82 to keep timing within hours.

docs.title: 6. Current production configuration (promoted 2026-10-27)
docs.text:
Written to data/telemetry/ml_calibration_state.json (backup taken). Replaces the prior round-2 LM params (NSE=0.45).

Parameter Value Meaning alpha_k 0.60 Muskingum K × baseline (faster, sharper routing) alpha_lag 0.82 basin lag × baseline (timing-faithful) muskingum_x 0.30 Muskingum X (higher → less attenuation, higher peak) delta_cn 0.0 per-subbasin CN preserved (61–75; AMC-III eff. 78–87) ia_frac 0.05 SCS initial abstraction fraction (saturated monsoon) uh_max_hr 90 unit-hydrograph duration cap uh_m_exp 20 unit-hydrograph shape exponent (sharp peak)

Per-subbasin CN and per-reach K/X are physically differentiated (not a single global value). Confidence 92%. Caveat recorded: do not chase 2021 with parameter tuning — see §5.3.

docs.title: 7. Agreed next steps
docs.text:
1. Correct the WRD rating curve at flood flows (user decision, §5.1): the reported flood stages (546.97 / 547.83 m) are authoritative, so a ~2150 m³/s flood maps to ~547 m, not ~542.6 m. Re-anchor / re-derive the Rajaram rating above ~542.7 m and re-evaluate the model's flood-stage accuracy on the corrected rating.
  2. Obtain better 2019/2021 rainfall forcing (gauge / orographic-corrected) to remove the Open-Meteo inversion (§5.3) and improve the 2019/2021 discharge agreement.
  3. Operational backwater buffer: flag forecasts for a ≤1 m upward adjustment when the Krishna gauge is high (§5.2).
  4. Re-validate on the corrected rating before any further production promotion.

docs.title: 5. State Synchronization, SWR & Vercel Serverless Architecture
docs.text:
Data fetching is wrapped through the client abstraction frontend/lib/api.ts:

export async function fetchDashboardData(runId?: string) {
  const query = runId ? `?run_id=${encodeURIComponent(runId)}` : "";
  const url = typeof window !== "undefined" 
    ? `/api/v1/dashboard${query}` 
    : `${BASE}/api/v1/dashboard${query}`;
  const res = await fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("API route response not ok");
  return await res.json();
}

docs.title: 5.1 Vercel Serverless Edge Bundling
docs.text:
On Vercel, serverless function workers execute isolated from external project folders (../data/runs/ is not packaged). To guarantee 100% production reliability:

  • All historical computation runs (CYC_*.json) and runs_index.json are mirrored into frontend/public/data/runs/.
  • When /api/v1/dashboard?run_id=... is called, the serverless handler resolves path.join(process.cwd(), "public", "data", "runs",${requestedRunId}.json), instantly serving the archived run without 404s or empty metrics.

docs.title: 5.2 Hydration Exception Hardening
docs.text:
All metric formatters in AccuracyPanel.tsx and SystemPanel.tsx are safely guarded:

ρ = {spearmanRho != null ? spearmanRho.toFixed(3) : "—"} · R² = {pearsonR2 != null ? pearsonR2.toFixed(3) : "—"}

This prevents TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'toFixed') during initial hydration or when inspecting runs with incomplete lead hours.

docs.title: 6. Peak Flood Strike Horizon & Permissible Uncertainty Window UI

To provide municipal emergency coordinators with actionable disaster timelines rather than ambiguous single-point predictions, DischargeDetailsCard.tsx and OverviewPanel.tsx render a dedicated early warning card:

docs.title: 7. Containerized Standalone Production Deployment (frontend/Dockerfile)
docs.text:
The frontend is containerized using a multi-stage Docker build leveraging Next.js standalone output:

# Stage 1: Dependency Installation
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

# Stage 2: Production Build
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
ENV NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED 1
RUN npm run build

# Stage 3: Minimal Production Runner
FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV production
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/static ./.next/static
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

This reduces the final container image footprint to \(< 180\text{ MB}\) and ensures zero external system dependencies.

docs.title: 10. Animated Visitor Odometer Counter (OdometerCounter.tsx)

The dashboard header and sidebar render an animated odometer with smooth mechanical digit transitions. It shows unique visits today and all-time visits from the persisted visitor ledger (Supabase, Upstash/KV, or the FastAPI backend).

  • Counts refresh every 60 seconds (and when the tab becomes visible) via GET /api/v1/visits/record, which never records a visit.
  • Responses are explicitly uncacheable, and the widget never uses hardcoded baselines or localStorage snapshots — so the displayed values cannot go stale.

The central Overview Panel features a fully interactive spatial mapping engine built using Leaflet.js and react-leaflet. It visualizes the spatial distribution of the flood model:

  • River Reaches: Plots the main stem of the Panchganga River and its 5 primary routing reaches as vector PolyLines.
  • Real-Time Rain Gauge Markers: Overlays the 18 physical IoT rain gauge stations with active telemetry indicators (e.g., flashing red for extreme precipitation zones).
  • Basemap: Uses a dark-mode styled topographic/satellite tile layer to ensure high contrast with the flood warning indicators and hydrologic boundaries.

docs.title: 1. Directory Structure & File Manifest
docs.text: The geospatial repository contains both raw QGIS spatial layers and web-optimized GeoJSON files:

docs.title: 2. Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS) Specification
docs.text:
Hydrologic vector processing uses dual spatial reference frames:

  1. Analytical Hydrologic Projected CRS: EPSG:32643 (UTM Zone 43N)
  2. Units: Meters (\(m\))
  3. Spheroid: WGS 84
  4. Usage: Used in GIS preprocessing for exact planimetric area calculation (\(\text{Area } A = \iint dx\,dy\)), channel length measurement (\(L\)), and reach slope determination (\(\Delta z / \Delta L\)).
  5. Web Map Geographic CRS: EPSG:4326 (WGS 84 Lat/Long)
  6. Units: Decimal degrees (\(^\circ\))
  7. Usage: Used for client-side Leaflet rendering, Open-Meteo coordinate queries, and GeoJSON serialization.

docs.title: 3. GeoJSON Feature Property Schemas
docs.text: Each layer carries only the properties the pipeline reads. Subbasin polygons carry subbasin_id (S1–S9), area_km2, curve_number, lag_hours and the Thiessen gauge list; reach centrelines carry reach_id (R1–R5), length_km, slope, muskingum_k_hours and muskingum_x. Anything else — labels, styling, survey notes — lives in the QGIS project and is not shipped to the runtime.

docs.title: Dual-Engine Hydrologic Strategy & HEC-HMS Automation
docs.text: HydroCast deploys a dual-engine hydrologic computing architecture designed for high-consequence operational flood forecasting across the 1,837.213 km² Panchganga River basin. The system pairs the gold-standard physical benchmark—the United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) HEC-HMS 4.13—with an in-house Pure-Python Vectorized Digital Twin Emulator (src/hms/runner.py).

docs.title: 1. Dual-Engine Technical Differentiation
docs.text:
The two engines serve distinct operational roles: native HEC-HMS provides regulatory institutional legitimacy and authoring verification, while the Python Twin provides sub-20 ms vectorized compute for real-time API responses, automated 6-hourly pipelines, and iterative Levenberg-Marquardt parameter optimization.

Engineering Dimension Native USACE HEC-HMS 4.13 Automation Pure-Python Vectorized Twin Emulator Primary Code Unit src/hms/runner.py::_execute_hec_hms_core src/hms/runner.py::compute_emulator_hydrograph Execution Medium Subprocess batch execution via headless Jython Pure Python 3 / NumPy vectorized matrix operations Control File Patched data/hms/HMS_Automation_RJKT/Control_1.control In-memory timestamp index (\(0 \dots \text{sim\_hours}-1\)) Automation Script Auto-generated compute.jy Direct Python in-process function invocation Input Forcing HEC-DSS binary file records via pydsstools Hyetograph array dictionary subbasin_hyetographs Execution Latency 14.8 – 15.2 seconds < 20 milliseconds (~750× speedup) Platform Portability Windows-centric (requires Java runtime & heclib.dll) 100% OS-agnostic (runs on Linux, macOS, Docker, CI) Reach Routing Stability Standard Muskingum; flags WARNING 41169 on long reaches Dynamic sub-stepping (\(N_{steps}\)); eliminates WARNING 41169 Volume Conservation May lose volume when \(C_0 < 0\) or \(C_2 < 0\) Guaranteed \(\sum Q_{\text{out}} = \sum Q_{\text{in}}\) within \(10^{-4}\) tolerance Primary Use Cases Authoritative desktop validation; regulatory compliance Real-time web API, Levenberg-Marquardt calibrator, CI/CD Output Run Status COMPLETED_BINARY CALIBRATED_RJKT

docs.title: 2.1 Project Layout & File Manifest
docs.text:
The authoritative HEC-HMS watershed model files reside in data/hms/HMS_Automation_RJKT/:

File Name Purpose & Physical Content HMS_Automation_RJKT.hms Master project definition linking basin, meteorology, and control specs. Basin_1.basin Authoritative catchment topology: 9 subbasins, 5 Muskingum reaches, junctions, and sinks. Basin_1.sqlite Geospatial SQLite cache containing delineated stream networks and subbasin boundaries. Control_1.control Simulation control specification: start/end dates, times, and 60-minute time step. Met_1.met Meteorological model specification for gage-based spatial precipitation interpolation. HMS_Automation_RJKT.gage Rain gauge registry referencing external meteorological time-series records. compute.jy Headless Jython automation script generated dynamically before execution. Run_1.dss Primary binary Direct Access Storage System (HEC-DSS) archive storing output hydrographs. Run_1.log Execution log file capturing engine convergence, routing steps, and warnings.

docs.title: 2.2 Binary Path Discovery (find_hec_hms)
docs.text:
The automation pipeline dynamically searches for local HEC-HMS installations:

  1. Environment Overrides: Checks HEC_HMS_PATH and HMS_HOME.
  2. Windows Installation Candidates:
  3. C:\Program Files\HEC\HEC-HMS\4.13\HEC-HMS.exe
  4. C:\Program Files\HEC\HEC-HMS-4.13\HEC-HMS.exe
  5. C:\Program Files\HEC\HEC-HMS-4.10\hec-hms.cmd
  6. Versions 4.12, 4.11, 4.10 in standard installation paths.
  7. Linux / Container Candidates:
  8. /opt/hec-hms/hec-hms.sh
  9. /usr/local/hec-hms/hec-hms.sh
  10. Failsafe Bypass: If HMS_FORCE_EMULATOR=1 is set in .env or PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST is present in the environment, native execution is bypassed in favor of the Python twin.

docs.title: 2.3 Dynamic Simulation Window Control & Restoration Pattern
docs.text:
To synchronize HEC-HMS execution with each 6-hourly cycle without permanently altering git-tracked configuration files, src/hms/runner.py uses a strict snapshot-patch-restore bracket pattern:

# 1. Snapshot pristine control specification into memory
snapshot_control_spec()

try:
    # 2. Patch simulation window for current forecast cycle (e.g. 03 Sep 2026 06:00 to 07 Sep 2026 00:00)
    patch_control_spec(start_dt, end_dt, time_step_min=60)

    # 3. Write Jython automation script
    write_jython_script(hms_dir, project_name="HMS_Automation_RJKT", run_name="Run 1")

    # 4. Launch headless subprocess
    subprocess.run([hms_bin, "-s", "compute.jy"], cwd=hms_dir, check=True, timeout=300)
finally:
    # 5. Guaranteed restoration: pristine control spec written back to disk
    restore_control_spec()

docs.title: 2.4 Headless Jython Automation (compute.jy)
docs.text:
The Jython execution script targets the official HEC-HMS 4.13 Java API:

# HEC-HMS 4.13 Batch Compute Script (compute.jy)
from hms.model.Project import Project

print "Opening HEC-HMS Project: E:/hydrocast_complete/data/hms/HMS_Automation_RJKT/HMS_Automation_RJKT.hms"
project = Project.open("E:/hydrocast_complete/data/hms/HMS_Automation_RJKT/HMS_Automation_RJKT.hms")

print "Executing simulation run: Run 1"
project.computeRun("Run 1")

print "Closing HEC-HMS Project..."
project.close()
print "HEC-HMS Computation Finished Successfully."

docs.title: 2.5 HEC-DSS Six-Part Pathname Architecture
docs.text:
Input precipitation hyetographs and computed discharge hydrographs are archived in USACE HEC-DSS binary format using pydsstools. Record identifiers follow the standardized six-part convention:

  / A / B / C / D / E / F /
  • Part A (Project / Basin): PANCHGANGA
  • Part B (Hydrologic Element): S1 through S9 (subbasins), R1 through R5 (reaches), or J_OUTLET (outlet junction)
  • Part C (Data Parameter): PRECIP-INC (incremental rainfall, mm) or FLOW (discharge, m³/s)
  • Part D (Start Timestamp): e.g. 03SEP2026:0600
  • Part E (Sampling Interval): 1HOUR
  • Part F (User / Version Qualifier): FORECAST, OBSERVED, or RUN:RUN_1

docs.title: 3. Pure-Python Vectorized Digital Twin Emulator
docs.text:
Implemented in src/hms/runner.py::compute_emulator_hydrograph, the digital twin reproduces the full hydrologic continuum across all 9 subbasins and 5 reaches in less than 20 milliseconds.

| Subbasin | Area (km²) | CN | Lag (min) | Routes To | Reach | K (hr) | X | Passes |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| S6 Gaganbawda | 227.72 | 61.78 | 3318 | R5 | R5 | 4.619 | 0.20 | 2 |
| S7 Garivade | 195.39 | 61.28 | 3362 | R5 | R5 | 4.619 | 0.20 | 2 |
| S9 Radhanagari | 366.97 | 64.31 | 5199 | R4 | R4 | 1.224 | 0.20 | 1 |
| S8 Beed | 177.44 | 65.76 | 3387 | R2 | R2 | 11.827 | 0.20 | 5 |
| S4 Karanjphen | 262.00 | 61.89 | 3116 | R3 | R3 | 3.829 | 0.20 | 2 |
| S5 Padasali | 106.39 | 60.97 | 2117 | R3 | R3 | 3.829 | 0.20 | 2 |
| S3 Kotoli | 261.32 | 64.82 | 3998 | R1 | R1 | 2.899 | 0.20 | 2 |
| S2 Sangarul | 153.77 | 65.74 | 3154 | R1 | R1 | 2.899 | 0.20 | 2 |
| S1 Karveer | 86.213 | 74.85 | 2152 | Sink-1 (direct) | — | — | — | — |

**Reach cascade:** R5 → R4 → R2 → R3 → R1 → Sink-1 (Rajaram Weir), with S1 flowing directly to Sink-1.

**Sink-1 outputs:** Routed surface outflow + direct S1 runoff + baseflow recession Q_bf(t).

### 3.1 Dynamic Antecedent Moisture Condition (AMC) Tracking

Soil moisture state dynamically scales Curve Numbers using TR-55 non-linear transformations based on the 90-hour basin-mean precipitation $\bar{P}_{90h}$:

$$\text{AMC} = \begin{cases} \text{AMC-I (Dry)} & \text{if } \bar{P}_{90h} < 25.0\text{ mm} \\ \text{AMC-II (Normal)} & \text{if } 25.0 \le \bar{P}_{90h} < 65.0\text{ mm} \\ \text{AMC-III (Saturated)} & \text{if } \bar{P}_{90h} \ge 65.0\text{ mm} \end{cases}$$

Non-linear Curve Number adjustments:

$$CN_{\text{I}} = \frac{4.2 \cdot CN_{\text{II}}}{10.0 - 0.058 \cdot CN_{\text{II}}}, \qquad CN_{\text{III}} = \frac{23.0 \cdot CN_{\text{II}}}{10.0 + 0.13 \cdot CN_{\text{II}}}$$

Initial abstraction $I_a = f_{ia} \cdot S$, where $S = \frac{25400}{CN} - 254$ mm, with dynamic fractions:
- $f_{ia} = 0.20$ for AMC-I
- $f_{ia} = 0.15$ for AMC-II
- $f_{ia} = 0.08$ for AMC-III

Incremental precipitation excess $\Delta P_{excess}(t) = \max\left(0, Q_{cum}(t) - Q_{cum}(t-1)\right)$.

### 3.2 Dimensionless Unit Hydrograph Transform

For each subbasin lag time $t_{lag} = \text{lag\_min} / 60.0$ hours:

$$t_p = 0.5 \Delta t + t_{lag} = 0.5 + t_{lag} \quad (\text{hours})$$

$$UH(t) = \left(\frac{t}{t_p}\right)^m \exp\left[m \left(1 - \frac{t}{t_p}\right)\right], \quad m = 3.7$$

The unit hydrograph is normalized so that total volume equals subbasin drainage area:

$$\int_0^\infty UH(t) \, dt = Area_{km^2} \times 10^3 \, \text{m}^3$$

Direct surface runoff is computed via discrete convolution:

$$Q_{direct}(t) = \sum_{\tau=0}^t \Delta P_{excess}(\tau) \cdot UH(t - \tau)$$

---

## 4. Elimination of HEC-HMS WARNING 41169 via Sub-Stepped Routing

### 4.1 Root Cause of WARNING 41169

In standard HEC-HMS 4.13 simulations, Muskingum reach routing uses fixed parameter pairs: travel time $K$ (hours) and dimensionless weighting factor $X$ (typically $0.20$).

The classic Muskingum recurrence equation is:

$$O_t = C_0 I_t + C_1 I_{t-1} + C_2 O_{t-1}$$

Where routing coefficients are:

$$C_0 = \frac{\Delta t - 2 K X}{2 K (1 - X) + \Delta t}, \quad C_1 = \frac{\Delta t + 2 K X}{2 K (1 - X) + \Delta t}, \quad C_2 = \frac{2 K (1 - X) - \Delta t}{2 K (1 - X) + \Delta t}$$

For numerical stability and physical validity, the routing time interval $\Delta t$ must satisfy the Courant-Muskingum stability band:

$$2 K X \le \Delta t \le 2 K (1 - X)$$

When $\Delta t < 2 K X$, coefficient $C_0$ becomes **negative**. Conversely, when $\Delta t > 2 K (1 - X)$, coefficient $C_2$ becomes **negative**.

In the Panchganga basin, reach **R2 (Middle Panchganga Trunk)** has $K = 11.827$ hr and $X = 0.200$. With a standard 1-hour simulation time interval ($\Delta t = 1.0$ hr):

$$\Delta t - 2 K X = 1.0 - 2(11.827)(0.200) = 1.0 - 4.731 = -3.731 < 0 \implies C_0 = -0.187 < 0$$

HEC-HMS logs this critical error:
WARNING 41169: Muskingum reach R2 parameters K=11.827 and X=0.200 violate stability criteria. C0 is negative (-0.187). Numerical oscillations and mass loss may occur. 
Negative coefficients cause artificial numerical dips below zero, unphysical wave deformation, and catastrophic loss of volume conservation.

### 4.2 Dynamic Sub-Stepping Algorithm

HydroCast's twin emulator resolves this by dynamically calculating the permissible sub-divided travel time $K' = K / N_{steps}$ such that both stability bounds are simultaneously satisfied:

$$K_{lim,hi} = \frac{\Delta t}{2 X} \implies N_{steps} \ge \left\lceil \frac{K}{K_{lim,hi}} \right\rceil$$

$$K_{lim,lo} = \frac{\Delta t}{2 (1 - X)} \implies N_{steps,lo} \ge \left\lfloor \frac{K}{K_{lim,lo}} \right\rfloor$$

$$N_{steps} = \max\left(1, \min\left(\left\lceil \frac{K}{K_{lim,hi}} \right\rceil, \left\lfloor \frac{K}{K_{lim,lo}} \right\rfloor\right)\right)$$

### 4.3 Reach Sub-Step Coefficient Matrix and Mass Conservation

The canonical reach parameters $K$ and $X$ are defined in [Catchment Hydrology: Muskingum Reaches](basin-hydrology.md#muskingum-reaches). Based on these values, the dynamic sub-stepping algorithm evaluates the following coefficient matrix:

| Routing Reach | River Segment | Sub-Step Passes ($N_{steps}$) | Sub-Divided $K'$ (hr) | $C_0$ | $C_1$ | $C_2$ | Numerical Stability Impact |
|:---:|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **R5** | Upper Kumbhi / Dhamani | **2 passes** | 2.310 | 0.016 | 0.410 | 0.574 | Non-negative ($C_0, C_1, C_2 \ge 0$) |
| **R4** | Bhogawati River Trunk | **1 pass** | 1.224 | 0.174 | 0.509 | 0.317 | Courant condition satisfied |
| **R2** | Middle Panchganga Reach | **5 passes** | 2.365 | 0.011 | 0.407 | 0.582 | **WARNING 41169 Eliminated** |
| **R3** | Kasari River Main | **2 passes** | 1.915 | 0.057 | 0.432 | 0.511 | Non-negative ($C_0, C_1, C_2 \ge 0$) |
| **R1** | Lower Panchganga Trunk | **2 passes** | 1.450 | 0.126 | 0.478 | 0.396 | Confluence cascade stabilized |

Because every sub-step satisfies $C_0 \ge 0$, $C_1 \ge 0$, $C_2 \ge 0$, and $\sum C_i \equiv 1.000000$, total volume is strictly conserved across all reaches:

$$\sum_{t=0}^{89} Q_{out}(t) = \sum_{t=0}^{89} Q_{in}(t) \quad \left(\text{Relative error } < 10^{-4}\right)$$

This mathematical guarantee is verified on every test execution in `tests/test_runner_emulator.py`.

---

## 5. Golden Regression Baseline (`tests/test_golden_emulator.py`)

To ensure that future enhancements, dependency updates, or calibration refactorings cannot introduce silent numerical drift, HydroCast maintains an automated **golden regression lock**.

### 5.1 Frozen Baseline Values

For a standardized deterministic monsoon storm peaking at hour 30 with $91.1\text{ m}^3/s$ initial baseflow:

| Metric | Golden Baseline Value | Tolerance | Test Assertion |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Antecedent Moisture Condition** | `AMC-III` | Exact string match | `assert hg["amc"] == "AMC-III"` |
| **Peak Lead-Time Hour** | $T = 105\text{ hr}$ | Exact integer match | `assert hg["peak_h"] == 105` |
| **Peak Outlet Discharge ($Q_{peak}$)** | **$3,345.6\text{ m}^3/s$** | $\pm 0.5\%$ relative | `pytest.approx(3345.6, rel=0.005)` |
| **Total Hydrograph Volume ($V_{total}$)** | **$754.115\text{ MCM}$** | $\pm 0.5\%$ relative | `pytest.approx(754.115, rel=0.005)` |
| **Surface Runoff Volume ($V_{surface}$)** | **$704,719,669.7\text{ m}^3$** | $\pm 0.5\%$ relative | `pytest.approx(704719669.7, rel=0.005)` |

### 5.2 Determinism Verification

The emulator contains zero unseeded stochastic elements or random variations. The determinism assertion:

```python
def test_emulator_is_deterministic():
    a = _run()
    b = _run()
    assert np.array_equal(a["q_total"], b["q_total"])
    assert np.array_equal(a["q_surface"], b["q_surface"])

Verifies that back-to-back evaluations yield bit-identical arrays across all 90 forecast time steps.

docs.title: Execution decision tree
docs.text: The module prefers the native HEC-HMS binary when it is present and runnable, and falls back to the Python emulator otherwise. The binary is used to produce the DSS artefacts and the run log; the numbers written into the forecast always come from the emulator, because the binary's results are never parsed back. This is a deliberate choice recorded in the errors register, not an oversight.

docs.title: Emulator internals
docs.text: The emulator walks the same three-stage chain as the HEC-HMS project: SCS Curve Number loss per subbasin, SCS unit hydrograph convolution to a subbasin hydrograph, and Muskingum routing along each reach. It reads its parameters from Basin_1.basin through the same parser the calibration engine uses, so the two can never disagree about the model definition.
